prompt.en: A path sketch is revised with both a higher refracting region and a higher antenna launch angle. What can be concluded about the first return point?

text.en: The return moves farther away because the higher region lengthens the path even at the steeper launch angle.

feedback.en: Greater region height lengthens the path at fixed angle, but the angle also changed. Its opposing effect cannot be discarded without comparing the changes.

text.en: The return moves closer because the steeper launch angle shortens the path even with the higher region.

feedback.en: A higher angle shortens skip at fixed region height, but region height also rose. The sizes of both changes matter.

text.en: The return stays in the same place because higher altitude and a steeper angle produce equal distance changes.

feedback.en: Opposing trends do not establish equal effects. Their magnitudes are needed before estimating the net movement.

text.en: The two changes act in opposite directions, so their net effect needs more information.

feedback.en: More height tends to lengthen skip while a higher launch angle tends to shorten it. Neither fixed-condition rule settles the combined change.

explanation.en: Keep the fixed conditions attached to each trend. A combined change needs more geometry than either trend alone.

prompt.en: A shoreline ground-wave route is moved much higher in frequency while the checkpoints stay fixed. Which revised expectation fits?

text.en: Useful surface-wave coverage may shrink, so the old checkpoint route may need a different band or path.

feedback.en: Ground wave is most useful at lower frequencies. The same checkpoint route may need a lower band or a different path.

text.en: Higher frequency should follow the shoreline more closely and extend surface-wave coverage.

feedback.en: That reverses the frequency trend. Higher-frequency ground wave generally becomes less useful over the same surface route.

text.en: A higher band should replace the surface path with a useful F2 return at the old checkpoints.

feedback.en: A sky-wave path depends on ionization and geometry as well as frequency. It need not cover the former surface-wave checkpoints.

text.en: Allow for smaller antennas but keep the earlier surface-wave coverage estimate.

feedback.en: The frequency change affects propagation, not just antenna dimensions. The former coverage estimate needs rechecking.

explanation.en: Do not carry a coverage map from a lower-frequency surface path onto a much higher band without new evidence.

prompt.en: A multi-hop sketch adds enough hop distance to span a route. Which assessment of its backup coverage is justified?

text.en: Once a single hop works at the chosen frequency, the remaining hops should have similar conditions and losses.

feedback.en: One usable hop does not establish the conditions along the rest of the route. Additional surface returns also introduce losses rather than simply repeating the first hop's link budget.

text.en: Each extra surface return can add loss, and the required ionospheric path still has to exist.

feedback.en: A geometrically long enough plan can still fail when conditions or link strength are unsuitable.

text.en: Surface reflections largely restore the signal, so hop count adds little to the loss budget.

feedback.en: A surface reflection redirects part of the arriving energy. It does not regenerate losses accumulated along the path.

text.en: A modest power reserve should make up for uncertainty in where the planned hops return.

feedback.en: Power can improve link strength along a usable path. It does not control the return geometry or replace a missing path.

explanation.en: Hop scales support an initial plan. Listening and path evidence are still needed before relying on it.
